claim: Rev-erbs repress subsets of genes that are activated by TLR ligands, IL4, TGFβ, and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPS).
source: Rather than reinforcing a specific program of macrophage polarization, Rev-erbs repress subsets of genes that are activated by TLR ligands, IL4, TGFβ, and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPS).
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by RNA-Seq data comparing WT and Rev-erb DKO macrophages under various stimulation conditions shown in Figure 1.

claim: A complex damage signal promotes co-localization of NF-κB, Smad3, and Nrf2 at Rev-erb-sensitive enhancers.
source: Unexpectedly, a complex damage signal promotes co-localization of NF-κB, Smad3, and Nrf2 at Rev-erb-sensitive enhancers and drives expression of genes characteristic of multiple polarization states in the same cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data showing co-localization of these transcription factors at enhancers following tissue homogenate treatment, as shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: Rev-erb-sensitive enhancers integrate multiple damage-activated signaling pathways to promote a wound repair phenotype.
source: Rev-erb-sensitive enhancers thereby integrate multiple damage-activated signaling pathways to promote a wound repair phenotype.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by RNA-Seq, ChIP-Seq, and in vivo wound healing data showing that Rev-erb deficiency leads to accelerated wound healing and altered gene expression patterns.

claim: Macrophages serve as sentinels of infection and injury and are active participants in both innate and adaptive immune responses.
source: As immune cells, macrophages serve as sentinels of infection and injury and are active participants in both innate and adaptive immune responses.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in immunology, representing general scientific knowledge about macrophage function.

claim: Detection of pathogens and tissue damage is mediated by a diverse array of pattern recognition receptors for pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and damage associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), exemplified by the toll-like receptors (TLRs).
source: Detection of pathogens and tissue damage is mediated by a diverse array of pattern recognition receptors for pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and damage associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), exemplified by the toll-like receptors (TLRs).
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific knowledge about innate immune recognition mechanisms.

claim: Ligation of TLRs initiates profound changes in gene expression that include induction of chemokines, cytokines, anti-microbial peptides, and other factors that contribute to the innate immune response and influence adaptive immunity.
source: Ligation of TLRs initiates profound changes in gene expression that include induction of chemokines, cytokines, anti-microbial peptides, and other factors that contribute to the innate immune response and influence adaptive immunity (Ostuni et al., 2013; Lawrence and Natoli, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on TLR signaling.

claim: TLR4 ligation regulates gene expression through signal transduction pathways culminating in the activation of latent signal-dependent transcription factors, which include members of the nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB), interferon regulatory factor (IRF), and activator protein 1 (AP-1) families.
source: TLR4 ligation regulates gene expression through signal transduction pathways culminating in the activation of latent signal-dependent transcription factors, which include members of the nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB), interferon regulatory factor (IRF), and activator protein 1 (AP-1) families (Medzhitov and Horng, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on TLR4 signaling pathways.

claim: In macrophages, signal-dependent transcription factors are primarily directed to macrophage-specific enhancers that are selected by macrophage lineage determining transcription factors, PU.1 and CCAAT-enhancer-binding proteins (C/EBPs).
source: In macrophages, these factors are primarily directed to macrophage-specific enhancers that are selected by macrophage lineage determining transcription factors, PU.1 and CCAAT-enhancer-binding proteins (C/EBPs) (Heinz et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on macrophage enhancer selection.

claim: The macrophage activation phenotype resulting from selective treatment with LPS, or in some cases a combination of LPS and interferon γ (IFNγ), is referred to as M(LPS) or M(LPS+IFNγ) activation.
source: The macrophage activation phenotype resulting from selective treatment with LPS, or in some cases a combination of LPS and interferon γ (IFNγ), is referred to as M(LPS) or M(LPS+IFNγ) activation (Murray et al., 2014), and is considered vital for the host response to bacterial or viral infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to literature on macrophage polarization nomenclature.

claim: TGFβ is generally considered to be an inducer of a 'de-activated' macrophage or M(TGFβ) phenotype.
source: TGFβ is generally considered to be an inducer of a 'de-activated' macrophage or M(TGFβ) phenotype, although it also acts as a potent chemo-attractant for monocytes and can potentiate their transition into activated cells (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on TGFβ effects on macrophages.

claim: Phagocytosis of apoptotic cells results in increased macrophage-mediated secretion of TGFβ and subsequent inhibition of inflammatory cytokine production.
source: For example, phagocytosis of apoptotic cells results in increased macrophage-mediated secretion of TGFβ and subsequent inhibition of inflammatory cytokine production (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Secreted TGFβ plays key roles in accelerating wound healing and fibrosis.
source: In addition to dampening inflammatory responses, secreted TGFβ plays key roles in accelerating wound healing and fibrosis (Schuppan and Kim, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on TGFβ functions.

claim: TGFβ signal transduction pathways function primarily in a Mothers against decapentaplegic homolog (SMAD)-dependent manner through Smad2-, Smad3-, and Smad4-mediated activation, as well as Smad7-mediated inhibition.
source: At the transcriptional level, TGFβ signal transduction pathways function primarily in a Mothers against decapentaplegic homolog (SMAD)-dependent manner through Smad2-, Smad3-, and Smad4-mediated activation, as well as Smad7-mediated inhibition (Massagué, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on TGFβ signaling.

claim: Ligation of TGFβ receptors causes the localization of Smad3 to genomic loci containing lineage-determining transcription factors.
source: Like other signal-dependent transcription factors, ligation of TGFβ receptors causes the localization of Smad3 to genomic loci containing lineage-determining transcription factors (Mullen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on Smad3 genomic localization.

claim: IL4 acts through the IL4 receptor to activate signal transducer and activator of transcription 6 (Stat6).
source: IL4 acts through the IL4 receptor to activate signal transducer and activator of transcription 6 (Stat6) (Lefterova et al., 2010), which positively regulates gene expression upon binding to recognition elements in promoters and enhancers of target genes (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on IL4 signaling.

claim: IL4 signaling regulates genes that control tissue remodeling, phagocytosis, scavenging, and the arginase pathway.
source: IL4 signaling regulates genes that control tissue remodeling, phagocytosis, scavenging, and the arginase pathway.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about IL4 functions in macrophages.

claim: The macrophage activation phenotype resulting from selective treatment with IL4 is referred to as M(IL4) and is considered vital for the role of macrophages in wound repair.
source: The macrophage activation phenotype resulting from selective treatment with IL4 is referred to as M(IL4) and is considered vital for the role of macrophages in wound repair (Van Dyken and Locksley, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on macrophage polarization.

claim: In vivo, macrophages encounter diverse combinations of signals that can change over time in response to physiological or pathological processes such as tissue injury.
source: In vivo, macrophages encounter diverse combinations of signals that can change over time in response to physiological or pathological processes such as tissue injury.
evidence: This is a general statement about macrophage biology based on established knowledge.

claim: Combinations of signals can influence the transcriptional landscape of macrophages in an input-specific fashion.
source: Recent studies show that these combinations of signals can influence the transcriptional landscape of macrophages in an input-specific fashion (Lavin et al., 2014; Ginhoux et al., 2015; Gosselin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature on macrophage transcriptional responses.

claim: The Rev-erb nuclear receptor family consists of two members, Rev-erbα (also known as nuclear receptor subfamily 1, group D, member 1, NR1D1) and Rev-erbβ (also known as nuclear receptor subfamily 1, group D, member 2, NR1D2).
source: The Rev-erb nuclear receptor family consists of two members, Rev-erbα (also known as nuclear receptor subfamily 1, group D, member 1, NR1D1) and Rev-erbβ (also known as nuclear receptor subfamily 1, group D, member 2, NR1D2) (Rev-erbs), that regulate the expression of genes involved in the control of circadian rhythm (Preitner et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2008; Cho et al., 2012), metabolism (Raspé et al., 2002; Le Martelot et al., 2009; Feng et al., 2011; Solt et al., 2012), and inflammation (Fontaine et al., 2008; Gibbs et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature on Rev-erb functions.

claim: Rev-erbs mediate transcriptional repression through recruitment of the nuclear co-repressor (NCoR) and histone de-acetylase 3 (HDAC3) complex.
source: Rev-erbs mediate transcriptional repression through recruitment of the nuclear co-repressor (NCoR) and histone de-acetylase 3 (HDAC3) complex (Yin and Lazar, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on Rev-erb mechanism of action.

claim: Rev-erbs lack the carboxy-terminal (AF2) transactivation domain, which is required for recruitment of co-activators.
source: Rev-erbs lack the carboxy-terminal (AF2) transactivation domain, which is required for recruitment of co-activators (Durand et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on Rev-erb structure.

claim: Genome-wide location analysis of Rev-erbα and Rev-erbβ in macrophages revealed thousands of binding sites, the vast majority of which resided at macrophage-specific enhancer-like regions of the genome established by PU.1 and other macrophage lineage determining factors.
source: Genome-wide location analysis of Rev-erbα and Rev-erbβ in macrophages revealed thousands of binding sites, the vast majority of which resided at macrophage-specific enhancer-like regions of the genome established by PU.1 and other macrophage lineage determining factors (Lam et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work from the same laboratory.

claim: Rev-erbs function to suppress the activities of enhancers by repressing enhancer-directed transcription.
source: Gain and loss of function experiments indicated that Rev-erbs function to suppress the activities of these enhancers by repressing enhancer-directed transcription.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from previous gain and loss of function experiments cited in the text.

claim: Deletion of Rev-erbβ exons to generate a non-functional Rev-erbβ mRNA results in marked de-repression of Rev-erbα expression and increased expression of a DNA binding domain deleted form of Rev-erbα mRNA.
source: Deletion of Rev-erbβ exons to generate a non-functional Rev-erbβ mRNA results in marked de-repression of Rev-erbα expression and increased expression of a DNA binding domain deleted form of Rev-erbα mRNA (Sud et al., 2007) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–b.

claim: Deletion of Rev-erbα exons results in Rev-erbβ de-repression.
source: Similar effects can be seen following deletion of Rev-erbα exons (corresponding to the DNA-binding domain) with respect to Rev-erbβ de-repression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–b.

claim: Reduction of targeted Rev-erb exonic mRNA averaged 90% for Rev-erbα and 80% for Rev-erbβ.
source: Reduction of targeted Rev-erb exonic mRNA averaged 90% for Rev-erbα and 80% for Rev-erbβ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Activation of TLR3 with polyinosinic-polycytidylic acid (Poly I:C), TLR4 with Kdo2-lipid A (KLA), TLR1/2 with Pam3CSK4 (Pam3), and co-activation with KLA and IFNγ induced characteristic pro-inflammatory gene signatures in WT macrophages.
source: Activation of TLR3 with a synthetic double-stranded RNA analog, polyinosinic-polycytidylic acid (Poly I:C), TLR4 with Kdo2-lipid A (KLA), TLR1/2 with a synthetic triacylated lipopeptide, Pam3CSK4 (Pam3), and co-activation with KLA and IFNγ induced characteristic pro-inflammatory gene signatures (Figure 1b and d) in WT macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1b and d.

claim: IL4 or TGFβ stimulation of macrophages resulted in alternatively activated and de-activated gene profiles, respectively.
source: In contrast, IL4 or TGFβ stimulation of macrophages resulted in the expected alternatively activated and de-activated gene profiles, respectively (Figure 1b and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1b and d.

claim: For the majority of genes, the magnitude of differential expression between WT and Rev-erb DKO macrophages varied depending on the polarization state.
source: Comparing the gene expression signature from WT and Rev-erb DKO macrophages, for the majority of genes, the magnitude of differential expression between WT and Rev-erb DKO macrophages varied depending on the polarization state (Figure 1c), in some cases only being observed under basal conditions, and in other cases only observed in response to a particular stimulus.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data comparing WT and Rev-erb DKO macrophages under different conditions shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Gene ontology analysis of mRNAs exhibiting differential expression in at least one of the single polarizing conditions revealed significant enrichment for genes involved in the response to wounding.
source: Gene ontology analysis of mRNAs exhibiting differential expression (>1.5-fold de-repressed in DKO macrophages) in at least one of the single polarizing conditions revealed significant enrichment for genes involved in the response to wounding (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis results shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Genetic loss of Cx3cr1 and Arg1 has been shown to hinder efficient wound healing in mice.
source: Notably, genetic loss of Cx3cr1 and Arg1 has been shown to hinder efficient wound healing in mice (Campbell et al., 2013; Ishida et al., 2008), suggesting that mice lacking Rev-erbs in cells of hematopoietic origin might exhibit more rapid wound healing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Cx3cr1 and Arg1 functions in wound healing.

claim: Rev-erb deficiency in bone marrow derived hematopoietic cells resulted in accelerated wound closure.
source: We found from three independent experiments that Rev-erb deficiency in bone marrow derived hematopoietic cells resulted in accelerated wound closure (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by wound healing data from bone marrow transplant experiments shown in Figure 2a–b.

claim: Accelerated wound closure was especially apparent on days 2–6 post-injury.
source: This was especially apparent on days 2–6 post-injury (Figure 2a), consistent with Rev-erb deficiency resulting in a faster response during the immune phase of wound healing.
evidence: This claim is supported by wound healing data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Bone marrow reconstitution efficiency exceeded 94%.
source: Bone marrow reconstitution efficiency exceeded 94% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Wounds from the Rev-erb DKO chimeric mice displayed greater immune cell infiltration and faster wound healing progression, characterized by enhanced re-epithelialization and increased granulation tissue development.
source: Wounds from the Rev-erb DKO chimeric mice displayed greater immune cell infiltration and faster wound healing progression, characterized by enhanced re-epithelialization and increased granulation tissue development (Figure 2c), characteristics correlated with an accelerated immune response during wound healing.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Rev-erb DKO bone marrow transplanted mice displayed more macrophages at the wound site on day 4 post-injury.
source: In addition, Rev-erb DKO bone marrow transplanted mice displayed more macrophages at the wound site on day 4 post-injury (Figure 2d), while neutrophil persistence at the wound site remained similar between WT and Rev-erb DKO transplanted mice (Figure 2e).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Neutrophil persistence at the wound site remained similar between WT and Rev-erb DKO transplanted mice.
source: In addition, Rev-erb DKO bone marrow transplanted mice displayed more macrophages at the wound site on day 4 post-injury (Figure 2d), while neutrophil persistence at the wound site remained similar between WT and Rev-erb DKO transplanted mice (Figure 2e).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Matrigel migration assays show increased extravasation of Rev-erb DKO macrophages when compared to their WT counterparts.
source: Moreover, matrigel migration assays show increased extravasation of Rev-erb DKO macrophages when compared to their WT counterparts (Figure 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro migration assay data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis of circulating blood leukocytes from WT and Rev-erb DKO bone marrow transplanted animals showed no differences in the populations of Ly6Clow/Ly6Chigh circulating monocytes.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of circulating blood leukocytes from WT and Rev-erb DKO bone marrow transplanted animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–d) showed no differences in the populations of Ly6Clow/Ly6Chigh circulating monocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–d.

claim: Tissue injury of the skin, muscle, or organ systems induces an initial local inflammatory response, which is followed by subsequent regenerative processes involving macrophages and other immune cells, as well as mesenchymal stem cells.
source: Classically, tissue injury of the skin, muscle, or organ systems induces an initial local inflammatory response, which is followed by subsequent regenerative processes involving macrophages and other immune cells, as well as mesenchymal stem cells (Novak and Koh, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on wound healing processes.

claim: Tissue homogenate provides a complex signal derived from components of disrupted cells (damage associated molecular patterns; DAMPs), the skin microbiome (microbial associated molecular patterns; MAMPs), and factors residing in the extracellular matrix (e.g., TGFβ).
source: This tissue homogenate (tissue homog/TH) provides a complex signal derived from components of disrupted cells (damage associated molecular patterns; DAMPs), the skin microbiome (microbial associated molecular patterns; MAMPs), and factors residing in the extracellular matrix (e.g., TGFβ).
evidence: This is an inference about the composition of the tissue homogenate based on knowledge of what is present in skin tissue.

claim: The gene expression signature of tissue homogenate-stimulated macrophages showed both similarities and differences when compared to the responses observed after treatment with TLR agonists, IL4, or TGFβ.
source: The gene expression signature of tissue homogenate-stimulated macrophages showed both similarities and differences when compared to the responses observed after treatment with TLR agonists, IL4, or TGFβ (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data comparing different treatment conditions shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 5590 genes exhibited concordant changes in expression between in vivo wound biopsies and macrophages stimulated with tissue homogenate.
source: Although myeloid cells represent only a small fraction of the total cells analyzed in the wound biopsy, 5590 genes exhibited concordant changes in expression with those observed following stimulation of macrophages with tissue homogenate (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data comparing in vivo wounds and in vitro tissue homogenate treatment shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Gene ontology analysis of genes exhibiting concordant changes indicated significant enrichment for biological process terms related to response to wounding, immune response, and cell adhesion.
source: Gene ontology analysis of this set of genes indicated significant enrichment for biological process terms related to response to wounding, immune response, and cell adhesion (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis results shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Response to wounding was the most highly enriched gene ontology term associated with genes de-repressed greater than two-fold in Rev-erb DKO tissue homogenate treated macrophages.
source: Response to wounding was the most highly enriched gene ontology term associated with genes de-repressed greater than two-fold in Rev-erb DKO tissue homogenate treated macrophages (282) followed by immune response and taxis (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis results shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Tissue homogenate induces a Rev-erb-sensitive program of macrophage gene expression that substantially overlaps with the pattern of gene expression observed in response to wounding in vivo.
source: These results indicate that tissue homogenate induces a Rev-erb-sensitive program of macrophage gene expression that substantially overlaps with the pattern of gene expression observed in response to wounding in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-Seq data comparing in vivo wounds, in vitro tissue homogenate treatment, and Rev-erb DKO effects.

claim: Genes associated with distinct polarization states resulting from activation with single ligands but exhibiting co-expression following treatment with tissue homogenate can reflect co-expression at the single cell level.
source: Genes associated with distinct polarization states resulting from activation with single ligands but exhibiting co-expression following treatment with tissue homogenate could reflect co-expression at the single cell level or mutually exclusive expression in subpopulations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that was tested using single cell RT-Q-PCR experiments.

claim: A subset of genes from each category of polarization states is expressed in the majority of tissue homogenate-treated cells.
source: Notably, evaluating individual genes by column, a subset from each category of polarization states is expressed in the majority of cells (e.g., Cxcl1, Dusp4, Cx3cr1, Pf4) (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by single cell RT-Q-PCR data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Genes from each polarization state can be expressed at similar levels in the same cell.
source: Conversely, evaluating the total set of genes across individual cells, genes from each polarization state can be expressed at similar levels in the same cell (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by single cell RT-Q-PCR data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Clustering revealed two main groups that were distinguished by lack of detectable expression of Fos and Rela.
source: Of interest, clustering revealed two main groups that were distinguished by lack of detectable expression of Fos and Rela.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of single cell RT-Q-PCR data.

claim: Cells lacking Fos and Rela expression also exhibit reduced expression of subsets of genes in the M(LPS) or M(LPS+IFNγ), tissue homogenate, and transcription factor categories.
source: Cells lacking Fos and Rela expression also exhibit reduced expression of subsets of genes in the M(LPS) or M(LPS+IFNγ), tissue homogenate, and transcription factor categories.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of single cell RT-Q-PCR data.

claim: While there is substantial heterogeneity in gene expression at the single cell level, genes characteristic of M(LPS) or M(LPS+IFNγ), M(TGFβ), and M(IL4) polarization states can be co-expressed in individual cells.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that while there is substantial heterogeneity in gene expression at the single cell level, genes characteristic of M(LPS) or M(LPS+IFNγ), M(TGFβ), and M(IL4) polarization states can be co-expressed in individual cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from single cell RT-Q-PCR data.

claim: Treatment with tissue homogenate induced H3K27ac at ~2500 regions after 3 hr and ~5000 regions after 6 hr.
source: Treatment with tissue homogenate induced H3K27ac at ~2500 regions after 3 hr and ~5000 regions after 6 hr (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data for H3K27ac shown in Figure 5a.

claim: De novo motif analysis revealed binding sites for Nrf2, AP-1, and NF-κB motifs as among the most highly enriched sequences in tissue homogenate-induced H3K27ac regions.
source: De novo motif analysis revealed binding sites for Nrf2, AP-1, and NF-κB motifs as among the most highly enriched sequences in these regions (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis of H3K27ac ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Tissue homogenate induced a pattern of genomic binding sites for p65, Fos, and Smad3 that substantially differed from the pattern resulting from stimulation with the single ligands, KLA or TGFβ.
source: In each case, we observed that tissue homogenate induced a pattern of genomic binding sites that substantially differed from the pattern resulting from stimulation with the single ligands, KLA (p65 and Fos) or TGFβ (Smad3) (Figure 5c).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data comparing different treatment conditions shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Tissue homogenate-induced binding sites for p65, Fos, and Smad3 were highly associated with tissue homogenate-induced gain of H3K27ac.
source: These binding sites were also highly associated with tissue homogenate-induced gain of H3K27ac, consistent with their contribution to these changes in active chromatin (Figure 5d).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: PU.1 and Fos exhibit a high degree of constitutive binding.
source: PU.1 and Fos exhibit a high degree of constitutive binding, consistent with roles as pioneering factors that collaborate with each other and other macrophage lineage-determining factors, but also show quantitative changes in response to KLA and tissue homogenate.
evidence: This claim is based on ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 6a and inference about their roles as pioneering factors.

claim: Smad3 and p65 both exhibit strong signal-dependent increases in ChIP-Seq signal at the majority of their binding sites.
source: Smad3 and p65 both exhibit strong signal-dependent increases in ChIP-Seq signal at the majority of their binding sites.
evidence: This claim is based on ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: A subset of enhancer-like regions occupied by Smad3 in cells treated with TGFβ were occupied by p65 in cells treated with KLA.
source: First, a subset of enhancer-like regions occupied by Smad3 in cells treated with TGFβ were occupied by p65 in cells treated with KLA.
evidence: This claim is based on ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: In the context of tissue homogenate treatment, both p65 and Smad3 are simultaneously bound at regions that are occupied by only one factor under single ligand stimulation.
source: However, in the context of tissue homogenate treatment, both factors are simultaneously bound (Figure 6a, yellow boxes).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Tissue homogenate treatment leads to binding sites for p65 and Smad3 that are not observed following treatment with KLA or TGFβ, respectively.
source: Second, and consistent with the results presented in Figure 5c, tissue homogenate treatment leads to binding sites for p65 and Smad3 that are not observed following treatment with KLA or TGFβ, respectively (Figure 6a, blue boxes).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Many of the new binding sites for p65 co-localize with Smad3 and vice versa.
source: Furthermore, many of the new binding sites for p65 co-localize with Smad3 and vice versa.
evidence: This claim is based on ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Motif analysis of tissue homogenate-specific SMAD binding sites using TGFβ-specific SMAD sites as the background returned an NF-κB recognition motif as the second most highly enriched motif.
source: Consistent with these findings at individual genomic locations, motif analysis of tissue homogenate-specific SMAD binding sites (from Figure 5c) using TGFβ-specific SMAD sites as the background returned an NF-κB recognition motif as the second most highly enriched motif (Figure 7a).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis results shown in Figure 7a.

claim: In TGFβ-treated cells, p65 co-localized with 6% of the Smad3 peaks.
source: We observed ~7400 p65 peaks, 5465 of which overlapped with the 39,825 peaks for Smad3 observed in TGFβ-treated cells, representing an overlap with 6% of the Smad3 peaks (Figure 7b).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 7b.

claim: In homogenate-treated cells, p65 co-localized with 82% of the Smad3 binding sites.
source: In contrast, we observed 20,858 p65 peaks and 13,975 Smad3 peaks in homogenate-treated cells, with p65 co-localizing with 11,379 (82%) of the Smad3 binding sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data analysis.

claim: The complex tissue homogenate signal drives substantial co-localization of p65 with Smad3 that is not observed following selective treatment with TGFβ.
source: Therefore, the complex tissue homogenate signal drives substantial co-localization of p65 with Smad3 that is not observed following selective treatment with TGFβ.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from ChIP-Seq data comparing TGFβ and tissue homogenate treatments.

claim: The top enriched motif in tissue homogenate-specific SMAD sites is a binding site for NFE2L2, also known as Nrf2.
source: Unexpectedly, the top enriched motif in tissue homogenate-specific SMAD sites is a binding site for NFE2L2, also known as Nrf2 (Figure 7a).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis results shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Nrf2 is a latent basic leucine zipper (bZIP) protein that is activated in response to cell injury and inflammation, and regulates the expression of antioxidant proteins that protect against oxidative damage.
source: Nrf2 is a latent basic leucine zipper (bZIP) protein that is activated in response to cell injury and inflammation, and regulates the expression of antioxidant proteins that protect against oxidative damage (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on Nrf2 function.

claim: Evaluation of RNA-seq data from both the in vivo wound model and tissue homogenate-treated macrophages revealed upregulation of numerous Nrf2 target genes, including Txn1, Sod2, Hmox1, Prdx6, and Nqo1.
source: Evaluation of RNA-seq data from both the in vivo wound model and tissue homogenate-treated macrophages revealed upregulation of numerous Nrf2 target genes, including Txn1, Sod2, Hmox1, Prdx6, and Nqo1, suggesting that Nrf2 is activated in macrophages as part of the wound response (Figure 7d).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Tissue homogenate increased the genome-wide binding of Nrf2 at thousands of genomic locations.
source: These experiments demonstrated that tissue homogenate increased the genome-wide binding of Nrf2 at thousands of genomic locations, a substantial fraction of which were observed to overlap with the tissue homogenate-induced binding sites for p65, Fos, and Smad3 (e.g., Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data for Nrf2 shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Genomic occupancy of PU.1, Smad3, Nrf2, Fos, and p65 was most similar upon treatment of macrophages with the tissue homogenate signal.
source: This analysis revealed that genomic occupancy of PU.1, Smad3, Nrf2, Fos, and p65 was most similar upon treatment of macrophages with the tissue homogenate signal, whereas patterns of transcription factor binding were more varied upon treatment of macrophages with individual stimuli (Figure 7e).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Co-localization of transcription factors increased from 1.4% (893 peaks) in the vehicle state to 12.05% (7758 peaks) when cells were treated with tissue homogenate.
source: This approach demonstrated co-localization of only 1.4% (893) of peaks in the vehicle state, which increased to 12.05% (7758) overlap when cells were treated with tissue homogenate.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 7f and g.

claim: The combination of signals present in tissue homogenate induce co-binding of multiple transcription factors to enhancers that mediate the tissue injury response.
source: This eight-fold increase in co-localization suggests that the combination of signals present in tissue homogenate induce co-binding of multiple transcription factors to enhancers that mediate the tissue injury response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from ChIP-Seq data analysis.

claim: The IKK inhibitor VII inhibits NF-κB activity.
source: To address this question, we evaluated effects of chemical inhibitors of NF-κB, Smad3, and Nrf2 on gene expression in tissue homogenate-treated macrophages, using the IKK inhibitor VII to inhibit NF-κB activity, SB-43154 to inhibit TGFβ signaling, and glutathione to block the activation of Nrf2 (Figure 8a–c).
evidence: This is based on known pharmacological properties of the inhibitor.

claim: SB-43154 inhibits TGFβ signaling.
source: To address this question, we evaluated effects of chemical inhibitors of NF-κB, Smad3, and Nrf2 on gene expression in tissue homogenate-treated macrophages, using the IKK inhibitor VII to inhibit NF-κB activity, SB-43154 to inhibit TGFβ signaling, and glutathione to block the activation of Nrf2 (Figure 8a–c).
evidence: This is based on known pharmacological properties of the inhibitor.

claim: Glutathione blocks the activation of Nrf2.
source: To address this question, we evaluated effects of chemical inhibitors of NF-κB, Smad3, and Nrf2 on gene expression in tissue homogenate-treated macrophages, using the IKK inhibitor VII to inhibit NF-κB activity, SB-43154 to inhibit TGFβ signaling, and glutathione to block the activation of Nrf2 (Figure 8a–c).
evidence: This is based on known pharmacological properties of glutathione.

claim: Each transcription factor (NF-κB, Smad3, and Nrf2) contributes to the integrated response to tissue homogenate.
source: These studies support the idea that each factor contributes to the integrated response to tissue homogenate.
evidence: This conclusion is based on inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 8a-c.

claim: Activation of Cx3cr1 by tissue homogenate was decreased upon targeting the NF-κB, TGFβ receptor, and Nrf2 pathways.
source: For example, activation of Cx3cr1 by tissue homogenate was decreased upon targeting the NF-κB, TGFβ receptor, and Nrf2 pathways, supporting the involvement of all of these pathways in the regulation of this gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by inhibitor experiment data.

claim: Dusp5 activation was sensitive to NF-κB inhibition.
source: For instance, Dusp5 activation was sensitive to NF-κB inhibition (Figure 8a) while Nptx1 activation was unaffected by NF-κB inhibition (Figure 8a).
evidence: This claim is supported by inhibitor experiment data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Nptx1 activation was unaffected by NF-κB inhibition.
source: For instance, Dusp5 activation was sensitive to NF-κB inhibition (Figure 8a) while Nptx1 activation was unaffected by NF-κB inhibition (Figure 8a).
evidence: This claim is supported by inhibitor experiment data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Socs3 activation was sensitive to both inhibition of NF-κB and TGFβ receptor signaling.
source: Surprisingly, Socs3 activation was sensitive to both inhibition of NF-κB and TGFβ receptor signaling (Figure 8a and b) and Ctla2b was selectively sensitive to inhibition of TGFβ receptor signaling (Figure 8b).
evidence: This claim is supported by inhibitor experiment data shown in Figure 8a and b.

claim: Ctla2b was selectively sensitive to inhibition of TGFβ receptor signaling.
source: Surprisingly, Socs3 activation was sensitive to both inhibition of NF-κB and TGFβ receptor signaling (Figure 8a and b) and Ctla2b was selectively sensitive to inhibition of TGFβ receptor signaling (Figure 8b).
evidence: This claim is supported by inhibitor experiment data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: Established Nrf2 target genes Txn1 and Hmox1, which were induced by tissue homogenate, were repressed by glutathione co-treatment.
source: Established Nrf2 target genes Txn1 and Hmox1, which were also induced by tissue homogenate, were repressed by glutathione co-treatment (Figure 8c).
evidence: This claim is supported by inhibitor experiment data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: The Rev-erb agonist SR-9009 repressed a subset of genes in tissue homogenate-treated macrophages, exemplified by Cx3cr1, Gpr84, and Pgd.
source: Finally, we investigated the ability of the Rev-erb agonist SR-9009 to influence the responses to tissue homogenate. This agonist repressed a subset of genes in tissue homogenate-treated macrophages, exemplified by Cx3cr1, Gpr84, and Pgd (Figure 8d).
evidence: This claim is supported by agonist experiment data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Rev-erbs have been established to play general roles in the regulation of promoters of ubiquitously expressed genes such as Bmal that control the circadian rhythm.
source: Rev-erbs have been established to play general roles in the regulation of promoters of ubiquitously expressed genes such as Bmal that control the circadian rhythm (Preitner et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2008; Cho et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Rev-erb functions.

claim: The great majority of Rev-erb binding sites in macrophages are located at cell-specific enhancers, which are selected by macrophage lineage-determining factors such as PU.1.
source: However, the great majority of Rev-erb binding sites in macrophages are located at cell-specific enhancers, which are selected by macrophage lineage-determining factors such as PU.1 (Lam et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Rev-erbs function to repress a network of genes associated with the response to wounding.
source: Here, using loss of function, transcriptomic, and epigenetic analyses, we demonstrate that Rev-erbs function to repress a network of genes associated with the response to wounding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Rev-erb expression in cells derived from the bone marrow compartment resulted in accelerated wound healing in the skin.
source: Consistent with altered transcriptional responses observed in vitro, loss of Rev-erb expression in cells derived from the bone marrow compartment resulted in accelerated wound healing in the skin.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo wound healing experiments.

claim: In vivo, Rev-erb expression is circadian.
source: In vivo, Rev-erb expression is circadian (Cho et al., 2012), implying that the effects on macrophage gene expression observed in the present studies are likely to vary over the course of the day.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Rev-erbs may act in a circadian manner to regulate aspects of tissue macrophage gene expression required for the normal turnover of extracellular matrix, tissue remodeling, and wound healing.
source: Rev-erbs may thus act in a circadian manner to regulate aspects of tissue macrophage gene expression required for the normal turnover of extracellular matrix, tissue remodeling, and wound healing.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential physiological role of Rev-erbs.

claim: The consequences of loss of function of Rev-erbs were dependent on the specific polarizing signal.
source: By evaluating the consequences of Rev-erb deficiency on macrophage gene expression in response to distinct polarizing signals in vitro, we found that the consequences of loss of function of Rev-erbs were dependent on the specific polarizing signal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from RNA-Seq data comparing different treatment conditions.

claim: Rev-erbs co-localize with NF-κB p65 and AP-1 family member Fos at enhancers activated by TLR ligands.
source: Consistent with this, Rev-erbs co-localize with NF-κB p65 and AP-1 family member Fos at enhancers activated by TLR ligands, and with Smad3 at enhancers activated by TGFβ.
evidence: This claim is based on ChIP-Seq data showing co-localization of these factors.

claim: Rev-erbs co-localize with Smad3 at enhancers activated by TGFβ.
source: Consistent with this, Rev-erbs co-localize with NF-κB p65 and AP-1 family member Fos at enhancers activated by TLR ligands, and with Smad3 at enhancers activated by TGFβ.
evidence: This claim is based on ChIP-Seq data showing co-localization of these factors.

claim: The transcriptomic response of the macrophage to tissue homogenate overlaps significantly with the transcriptional response observed in a skin wound.
source: While the specific identities and concentrations of the DAMPs, MAMPs, and other bioactive molecules in this homogenate are unknown, we provide evidence that the transcriptomic response of the macrophage to this mixture overlaps significantly with the transcriptional response observed in a skin wound, thereby validating its use.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data comparing in vivo wounds and in vitro tissue homogenate treatment.

claim: The complex signal provided by tissue homogenate coordinately induces binding of NF-κB, AP-1, and Smad transcription factors.
source: Through ChIP-Seq experiments, we demonstrate that this complex signal coordinately induces binding of NF-κB, AP-1, and Smad transcription factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data.

claim: De novo motif analysis of activated enhancers led to the discovery that the tissue damage signal acutely activates Nrf2.
source: Furthermore, de novo motif analysis of activated enhancers led to the unexpected discovery that the tissue damage signal also acutely activates Nrf2.
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis and subsequent ChIP-Seq experiments for Nrf2.

claim: The use of glutathione to neutralize reactive oxygen species provides evidence for the functional importance of Nrf2 in the transcriptional response to the tissue damage signal.
source: Accordingly, the use of glutathione to neutralize reactive oxygen species, thus blocking the downstream disruption of the Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1)-Cuilin 3 (Cul3) complex required for activation of Nrf2 (Gorrini et al., 2013; Shibata et al., 2013) provides evidence for its functional importance in the transcriptional response to the tissue damage signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by inhibitor experiments and citations to literature on Nrf2 activation mechanisms.

claim: The use of inhibitors of NF-κB and TGFβ provided support for functionally important roles of these transcription factors.
source: Similarly, the use of inhibitors of NF-κB and TGFβ provided corresponding support for functionally important roles of these transcription factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by inhibitor experiments.

claim: The tissue homogenate signal induced different genomic locations of p65, Fos, and Smad3 than were observed following KLA or TGFβ.
source: Second, we found that the tissue homogenate signal induced different genomic locations of p65, Fos, and Smad3 than were observed following KLA or TGFβ, respectively, resulting in co-binding at a large number of enhancer-like regions in the vicinity of tissue homogenate-induced genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data comparing different treatment conditions.

claim: Transcription factor binding maps are context-dependent and must be interpreted accordingly.
source: An important implication of these findings is that transcription factors binding maps are context-dependent and must be interpreted accordingly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that transcription factor binding patterns differ depending on the stimulus.

claim: The observed co-localization of factors in response to the complex signal enables the appropriate integration of multiple relevant signaling components necessary for the initial acquisition of a wound repair phenotype.
source: We speculate that the observed co-localization of factors in response to the complex signal enables the appropriate integration of multiple relevant signaling components necessary for the initial acquisition of a wound repair phenotype (Figure 8e).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Delayed wound healing is observed in diabetics.
source: Delayed wound healing is observed in a number of pathological contexts, including in diabetics (Falanga, 2005; Sen et al., 2009) and in immunocompromised individuals (Chen et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Delayed wound healing is observed in immunocompromised individuals.
source: Delayed wound healing is observed in a number of pathological contexts, including in diabetics (Falanga, 2005; Sen et al., 2009) and in immunocompromised individuals (Chen et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Rev-erb antagonists could be evaluated as a means of enhancing wound repair in settings of delayed wound healing.
source: In these settings, it is possible that Rev-erb antagonists could be evaluated as a means of enhancing wound repair.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: A large number of devastating and largely untreatable diseases are characterized by exaggerated tissue fibrosis, such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, interstitial renal fibrosis, and liver fibrosis.
source: Alternatively, a large number of devastating and largely untreatable diseases are characterized by exaggerated tissue fibrosis, such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, interstitial renal fibrosis, and liver fibrosis (Schuppan and Kim, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A Rev-erb agonist can suppress a subset of genes that are de-repressed in the Rev-erb DKO and are regulated by the complex wound signal.
source: We demonstrate that a Rev-erb agonist can suppress a subset of genes that are de-repressed in the Rev-erb DKO and are regulated by the complex wound signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by agonist experiment data.

claim: Rev-erbs act to repress a specific combination of genes downstream of multiple signaling pathways that collectively function in an integrated manner to promote the response to wounding.
source: Overall, our findings suggest that Rev-erbs act to repress a specific combination of genes downstream of multiple signaling pathways that collectively function in an integrated manner to promote the response to wounding (Figure 8e).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data.

claim: It will be of interest to evaluate whether defects in Rev-erb signaling are associated with fibrotic diseases and whether pharmacological modulation of Rev-erb might be of therapeutic benefit.
source: It will therefore be of interest to evaluate whether defects in Rev-erb signaling are associated with these diseases and whether pharmacological modulation of Rev-erb might be of therapeutic benefit.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: The majority of Rev-erb binding sites identified in RAW264.7 macrophages co-localize with binding sites for their obligate co-repressor NCoR in BMDMs.
source: Furthermore, the majority of Rev-erb binding sites identified in RAW264.7 macrophages co-localize with binding sites for their obligate co-repressor NCoR in BMDMs, strongly suggesting that Rev-erbs occupy a similar cistrome in these cells (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of ChIP-Seq data for Rev-erbs in RAW264.7 cells and NCoR in BMDMs shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Enhancer analysis can be used to identify transcriptional mediators of unknown environmental factors.
source: This finding illustrates the utility of enhancer analysis to identify transcriptional mediators of unknown environmental factors, providing a basis for subsequent directed analysis of corresponding upstream signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a general methodological conclusion drawn from the discovery of Nrf2 involvement through enhancer motif analysis.
